paragraphs.text: The Lord has been helping us through our brother* in regard to the kind of persons who are capable of receiving divine communications. This is particularly seen in the beginning of Luke’s gospel where we have certain persons who received direct communications as to the current mind of heaven. Now I am sure that there is nobody here tonight but would value an increased ability to receive communications from God Himself as to what is in His mind currently.

We may know a good deal about the revealed mind of God in the Scriptures; we might know what He has done in the past; we might know—something and thank God we do know something—about God’s mind in relation to the future, but it is very important, beloved, to have some ability by the Spirit to receive something in the way of communication as to the present mind of God. I am sure we would all greatly value this.

Now it would be evident from Scripture that God does not care to communicate His mind to persons who are at a distance from Him. You will remember that in Numbers 11 the people murmured. Why did they murmur? I believe it was, dear brethren, that they were not in the current of God’s mind for the moment. They did not understand what God was doing, so they complained and murmured, and we are told in that
* see word printed in this Issue page 6

chapter that a certain number who were at the extremity of the camp were slain by the fire of God. That indicates that God is not interested in communicating His mind to persons who are content to remain at a distance from Him.

In Psalm 90, where we read that precious verse, we have Moses the man of God. I suppose there is not a better example in the whole of the Old Testament of a person who was capable of receiving direct communications from God than Moses. When Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses and complained against him in Numbers 12, God came down. He called the three out, Moses, Aaron, and Miriam. How ready God is to protect a man who is near to Himself. Such as are interested in His current mind—God will protect them. So He came down and challenged Aaron and Miriam. He said, “If there be a prophet among you, I Jehovah will make myself known to him in a vision, I will speak to him in a dream. Not so my servant Moses”, Numbers 12: 6. And then He says as to Moses, “He is faithful in all my house”. That is a word for us tonight, dear brethren. Our brother has been speaking to us in regard of what is distinctive and clear. How clear Moses was as to where he stood, and God said about Moses that he was faithful in all His house; not only in some things, not only in the things he liked most, but he was faithful in all God’s house.
Every detail of the truth came into expression in a man like Moses and God goes on to speak to Aaron and Miriam as to Moses, “Mouth to mouth do I speak to him”. The result of Moses’

knowledge of God, and of his nearness to God, was that God spoke to him mouth to mouth as a man speaks to his friend. Would you not like to receive divine communications? It is open to every one of us to get some impression of what the current mind of God is. So Moses says

in this psalm, “Lord, thou hast been our dwelling-place in all generations”. Think of God being a dwelling-place! Moses received the mind of God in regard to the building of the tabernacle, but he is not speaking of the tabernacle here as the dwelling-place, he is speaking of God Himself as being the dwelling-place. I think, dear brethren, that this wonderful privilege is open to all of us. The New Testament opens it up more fully, especially in John’s writings, that God becomes the dwelling-place of the heart. Every true lover of Christ can find a dwelling-place in God Himself, and that is what Moses is saying here.

David could say it, too. You will remember that David wanted to build God a house, a dwelling-place, and God sent Nathan the prophet to tell him that he could not build Him a house to dwell in (1 Chronicles 17: 4)—“Thy son that shall come out of thy loins, he shall build the house”, 2 Chronicles 6: 9. What did David do? He went in and he sat before Jehovah. David found a resting place, he found a home, he found all that his heart longed for, in the presence of God Himself. David could say with Moses, “Thou hast been our dwelling-place in all generations”. Think of that—what experiences the men had with God! Then if we think of the public side, what exercises there are to face in the testimony when things are broken down. Then conditions in the world are also to be felt by us. How serious the state of things in the world is at the present time. Yet Moses shows us the way that we can retire from the whole thing, and find a home. David showed the way to get into the presence of God and find rest and peace of mind; in the midst of the turmoil and the strain to find a resting place, a secure place.
The next psalm says, “He that dwelleth in the

secret place of the Most High”. What do we know, dear brethren, of the secret place? Paul writing to the Colossians says, “Your life is hid with the Christ in God”, Colossians 3: 3. It is not the time for public display; God never intended christianity to be on public display. I am not speaking against the proclamation of the glad tidings and the spread of them—may God spread them more—but God never intended that christianity as such should be on display in this dispensation. The time of display will come, but the time that we are in—let it sink into our hearts—is a time when we need to know the secret place. “He that dwelleth in the secret place of the Most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty”. Oh what security!

Beloved brethren, can we get together about it? Can we get nearer to one another about this secret place where God Himself is a refuge? God has been a dwelling-place through all generations. Paul speaks of generations; he says, “To him be glory in the assembly in Christ Jesus unto all generations”, Ephesians 3: 21. Moses knew God; he knew the God of Abraham, and of Isaac, and of Jacob, and he says, “Thou hast been our dwelling-place in all generations”. Here is Moses, a psalmist, and he is speaking of the great things of the Most High. You know, that lifts us up above the confusion, above the storm. When an aircraft goes up above a certain height it is above the storm, above the weather. What a thing it is to be lifted up into the secret place of the Most High and to be elevated into what is heavenly, as our brother has been saying—the heavenly possession that we have lifts us completely out of the confusion that exists in this poor scene.
Now I want to confirm this in the New Testament. In 1 John 4: 15 John says, “God abides in him”
That is a wonderful thing. The Lord Jesus says in John 14: 20, “In that day ye shall know that I am in my Father, and ye in me, and I in you”. Think of that; oh, what links of intimacy!

Dear brethren, let us go in for it. I am sure that the thing that will give us stability in any storm through which we may pass is our known and experienced links with God, “In that day ye shall know”— do we know, dear brethren? Let us know it better. “I am in my Father, and ye in me, and I in you”. Is that not wonderful? It is the secret place of the Most High; christianity is characterised by the revelation of God.

We are here tonight in this room in the full light of the revelation of God in Jesus. It is the time when the light is shining—the full light of the revelation of God. And who revealed Him? Where has the revelation come from? From a Man who was in the bosom of the Father; but He is there, and the light of the revelation of God is found in the face of a Man who is in the bosom of the Father. That is what gives character to christianity. It is the greatest conception that God has ever had on earth; He has it at the present time and it is in the light of the revelation of God in the face of a Man who is in the bosom of the Father. John’s first epistle opens up for us that Christ wants our companionship with Him there. Not that we can be in the unique place that He has in the bosom of the Father, but He wants us to be near to Him where He is. The current mind of God is that we should know our links and relations with Christ where He is, and that draws us into relationship with God.
This passage goes on to say, “And we have known and have believed the love which God has to us. God is love, and he that abides in love abides in God, and God in him”. Is not that wonderful?

I think that it is amazing—the human mind cannot take it in. We need the help of the Spirit to understand what the place of intimacy is into which God would bring us even at the present time. So let us covet, dear brethren, to get these communications. We will not get them if we are content to remain at a distance. If persons are content to allow things to come between them and God, to separate them from God, they will not understand the current mind of God.

It is revealed to those who are in nearness to Him. May the Lord help us to understand these relationships that are open to us, and with the relationship will come the communications that stabilise us in a day of trouble, for His name’s sake.
These are well-known scriptures and much referred to amongst us, especially Exodus 21

where the Hebrew bondman is a type of the Lord Jesus and His devotion. I want to refer briefly to two expressions in these passages which we all need to be affected by. First in verse 14 of Hebrews 11, “For they who say such things shay clearly that they seek their country”. It is a great matter that things should be shown clearly, that there should be no vagueness as to our part in the testimony, in the great things of God. The second passage is in Exodus 21: 5,
“But if the bondman shall say distinctly, I love my master, my

wife, and my children, I will not go free”. It is a great and important thing that matters should be distinct with us in our committal. We are living in difficult days and in the public body of profession we find many who are marked by a lack of showing clearly where they stand in relation to the great things of God, the things of the testimony, especially in regard to what is heavenly, and also there is a great lack of persons, believers maybe, saying things distinctly.
It is a great thing that there should be clarity in all that we are in our movements and all that we say in our confession of God’s testimony.

These persons in Hebrews are remarkable. Of course, the whole of Hebrews 11 is a marvellous chapter, opening up the world of faith. It is an important thing to understand the world of faith and to be in it as marked by that which marked these persons and their faith.
Hebrews 11: 16 is especially affecting where it says that God is not ashamed to be called their God; for He has prepared for them a city.

Dear brethren, we know a great deal of what it is for persons to be ashamed of us and to be ashamed to be linked with us in relation to our God, but it is very comforting and establishing to think that as we are in the path of faith, showing clearly where we belong. God is not ashamed of us to be called our God. That certainly is affecting, when we think of the years that have passed and all that we have gone through and got deliverance from, things in which we were once held, and what it has meant—it may be with some of us the loss of our families—to know that God is not ashamed to be called our God. How affecting that is, dear brethren! What a person Sarah was, for instance; how she paved the way for the incoming of Isaac, typical of Christ. What a

line of things is projected on to our view in Sarah’s faithful stand in relation to Isaac, over against the bondwoman’s son, the casting out of Ishmael making way for Isaac. How great that was in the divine mind. We think of Abraham too, and what is said of him, that he
“obeyed to go out” (Hebrews 11: 8). He is the father of us all, the great progenitor of faith—

of those who are marked by faith—and it says, “All these died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them from afar off and embraced them, and confessed that they were strangers and sojourners on the earth”. It is important, dear brethren, that we should be marked by strangership, pilgrims and strangers in a world where we have been socially and morally cast out.

It is a great thing to live as those who really belong to heaven. Our calling is heavenly and it says of these that, “They were strangers and sojourners on the earth. For they who say such things show clearly that they seek their country”. How fine that is! It says, “And if they had called to mind that from whence they went out, they had had opportunity to have returned”.

Surely we do not want to return to a world out of which we have been called—a world that has been judged in the death of Christ. In John 12: 31 the Lord refers to His exit out of this world by way of the cross. He says, “Now is the judgment of this world”. We have often said, and it is well to remember, that whilst the Lord died at the hands of wicked men, cruel hands which had to do with His crucifixion, we must always also remember that the Lord’s exit from the world was judicial. He had judged every principle of the world. He could not fit into the system that the world constituted. It was all dealt with judicially in the death of Christ.
We always need to remember that, and He would have us, as His own followers,
judge in our hearts every feature that had to be judged by Him in going into death, taking His exit judicially out of this world that God was having to say to.

It says, “but now they seek a better”; thank God for the better, dear brethren; it is truly “a better”. More and more, though it may be in outward weakness and smallness numerically, we are realising what this epistle so often speaks about as the ‘better’ things. It is a word that is constantly used in this epistle. It says that they had had opportunity to return, “but now they seek a better, that is, a heavenly; wherefore God is not ashamed of them, to be called their God”. What a God we have; “this God is our God”. How blessed, how lovely, to think of our God—that God is not ashamed to be called our God. We love to think of what it will be eternally when, as it says in Revelation 21: 3, “God himself shall be with them, their God”. How wonderful to think that now, with all the upheavals in the world and in the public bodies of profession, and the upheavals that we knew so well at one time—how blessed to think that in the area in which we are God is not ashamed to be called our God.

Now I refer to Exodus 21 briefly. What a wonderful type of Christ it is! How distinctly He said, “I love my master, any wife, and my children”. How He loved His God; what God was to Him, and what a place He filled out as a Bondman in complete committal to the will of God, unswerving in His obedience. How distinct He was as He said, “I love ... my wife, and my children”. How blessed these statements are! It is the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge; His complete, ardent devotion to God and to the assembly and to the saints—who would be affected by it. May we learn

to take on His spirit and to be marked by something, of His devotion, to have part in grace in the testimony and be able to say things distinctly, without a cloud, without a doubt, without anything that would mar the understanding of our saying distinctly, ‘I love my master, my wife, my children’. That is a full committal to God, to the assembly, and to all that is related to it.

It says his master “shall bring him before the judges, and shall bring him to the door, or to the door-post; and his master shall bore his ear through with an awl”. The judges and the doorpost are all suggestive of the administrative position. I think we might be affected by this, that as we have brought before us what Christ was, typically in the Hebrew bondman, in full and absolute devotion in love to His God and to the assembly, the whole administrative area is to be affected by this. On Lord’s day morning at the Supper the love of Christ for God and for the assembly is before us. He could say as to that holy vessel of God’s will, His body, “This is my body which is given for you”, Luke 22: 19.

Well, this is just the impression one has had today—one is affected by this matter of clearness of expression, saying distinctly what our love is as bound up in the testimony with others and declaring plainly the country we belong to, which is heavenly.

articles.title: “THE LIVING, THE LIVING, HE SHALL PRAISE THEE”
articles.author: A. J. E. Welch

paragraphs.text: In the bearing of this prophecy upon us we can say that Hezekiah was a man who was caused to experience life. The word had come to him from Jehovah, “Set thy house in order; for thou shalt die, and not live”—remarkably expressed, as if to set over against each other the great points of death on the one hand and life on the other. What we had on Lord’s day would give us the great basis of life—the quickening touch of Christ, operating in depth in our affections especially. The concern immediately now is just the measure of answer in life that there may be with each of us. I say each of us, because although the assembly is peculiarly in view, these elements of experience are personal to us, each one.

So we have Hezekiah before us, a king of whom much is said in the historical Scriptures that is to his credit, but what was needful was the experience and power of life. We might be in a path which bears a certain outward commendability; every commendable feature God takes account of; but what might be wanting at any time is the spring of life in the soul, leading to the element of praise—“The living, the living, he shall praise thee, as I this day”. That is, the one who writes is not only conveying that there are such persons, but he is conscious of being among them—“as I this day”. One feels what substance it would bring to our

gatherings together if each of us came in the spirit of this, as I this day”. It was the occasion of very deep exercise with Hezekiah, which he goes over item by item in this writing of his, when he had recovered from his sickness; he speaks of Jah in the land of the living (Isaiah 38: 11), getting a fresh view in his soul of God in relation to life.

One feels increasingly, dear brethren, the need of this touch of life, constantly sustained and refreshed in the soul, leading to prosperous conditions in local assemblies, to that delightful sensitiveness to the Spirit which is to be normal in every assembling of the saints. How fundamental this element of life is to prosperity in what is for Christ’s heart in the assembly!

But it has to be entered into on the basis of experience; and that experience in some sense will involve the experience of death. It was very real to Hezekiah to be told, “Thou shalt die, and not live”. It caused him to weep, and God saw his tears, and told him that He saw them.

It is a question, for the little time for which any one of us might remain, how that time shall be expended. Shall we be in the gain of what is really life? In referring to this I am not just dwelling upon the physical thing. It was clearly in view for Hezekiah that the fifteen years’

extension of life that he received should be spent in the gain of the deep exercise that he passed through at this time. How much there is to be known of God Himself in relation to what is living! He is indeed the living God; Christ is the Son of the living God (Matthew 16: 16), and that point relates to the assembly and its building, as if the whole great scope of things before us is related in the divine mind to life.
So Hezekiah says, “Lord, by these things men

live”; he refers back, I take it, to the elements of exercise through which he had passed. That is to say, there are to be no short cuts into the reality and power of life according to God, no lack of searching out according to the exercise that God would pass us through—“by these things men live”. We are brought to acknowledge, I suppose, as to every element of soul exercise through which we consciously pass, and in which we reach an issue, that it tends to life. So let us not be reluctant to go into matters before God, and with God, in the understanding that, in the very process of exercise that He delights to bring about, the tendency will be into life.

The times in which we live are marked by a certain characteristic depth of searching, and God is in that; but out of the searching He will bring great results, and the results shall be in life. We look back upon the searchings in the sense that what God is proceeding with through the searchings is a living order of things; and He would have us in the conscious experience and gain of it. “In all these things is the life of my spirit; and thou hast recovered me, and made me to live”. God had done that. We have to realise that it is God who does it. It is the quickening touch. We think of the quickening side of glory in the several Persons of the Godhead—the way that quickening power is linked with the Father, and with the Son, and with the Spirit. Each is able in some sense to make us to live, as if the whole glory of the Godhead is connected with this realm of life into which God would bring us.

Well, dear brethren, this is a matter more to be gone through in experience than to be spoken about at great length; but this indicates to us, I believe, a certain line which marks the present time, as God

is active to deepen His work in His saints. We have spoken to the Lord tonight about the beginnings of His work in the saints, and the wonderful initial operation of the Spirit in new birth; and God is showing us how things are to be developed, how the beginnings of His work come to fruition, to maturity. How attractive it is when maturity of life is presented under the eye of God in His saints, as the fruit of the experiences by which men are made to live. And the outcome is for God—“The living, the living, he shall praise thee, as I this day—the father to the children shall make known thy truth”. That is to say, this matter is to be transmitted through the course of the testimony, showing us the way in which the truth has been prospered amongst the saints.

Then Hezekiah says, “Jehovah was purposed to save me.—And we will play upon my stringed instruments all the days of our life, in the house of Jehovah”. It leads us to the house of Jehovah, and that with the stringed instruments, a delightful reference to the fruit of discipline, the fruit of pressure, maybe, that comes in upon us—“stringed instruments ... in the house”. You will notice how he expresses it ‘ We will play upon my stringed instruments’.

That is, as each one of us comes into the gain of these things, stringed instruments result which are available to the saints in a general sense, that what is precious to God may find its course for His praise in the assembly. Should we not, dear brethren, be a praising people in these days when the elements of life and power are so much becoming known in the midst of His saints? May there be a portion for Him from it.

Our brother has been speaking of the activities of assembly persons, of the characteristics of assembly persons, and what some of the activities of such persons might be. It appeals to me that one activity of assembly persons would be to seek to add something, characteristically to be adding something, which is for the glory of the Lord Jesus and for the upbuilding of the local company, the local assembly. That would be the outlook of assembly persons.

There is this word in Chronicles, “and thou shalt add to it”. We might say that characteristically David added; constantly in his life, from his earliest time, he added that which was for the glory of God. He says here “in my affliction I have prepared …” and he says elsewhere, “in my affection … I have prepared”, 1 Chronicles 29: 3. Characteristically, in all his experiences, in all his movements and the thoughts of his heart, he was always gathering something and adding something. What tremendous wealth he acquired! What wealth—we might say stupendous wealth—was acquired in David’s time. It says, “a hundred thousand talents of gold, and a thousand thousand talents of silver; and of brass and iron without weight, for it is in abundance”. In each experience, whether happy or sad—and he speaks of his affliction—he would say, ‘What is
there in this that will add to the glory of the blessed God?’. From his earliest time he had the concept that there was to be a resting place for the ark.

He brought humbling experiences upon himself, but I am sure that each time he did so he knew what it was to repent, to get into the presence of God as to what he had done. He would have said (putting it in christian language) ‘The ark is Christ in manhood, fulfilling all for the divine pleasure. I have turned aside—the ark is unique and glorious and would never turn aside’. He would thus be acquiring something—he was acquiring gold and silver literally, but for ourselves, beloved brethren, I have a deep sense that it is something formed in the soul, for the glory of God, of the perfection of Jesus, really known and enjoyed. We get the contrast between all that there is in that blessed Man and all that we have to judge in ourselves. We have had to say individually and as companies that we have gone astray. As our beloved brother said, we are in the house of Simon the leper characteristically, but is that to deflect us in any way? It is only to enhance the glory of the blessed One who never went astray, who was here in perfection for the pleasure of the blessed God in singleness of heart and devotion, and the love of the Lord Jesus for the Father, His devotion to His will, His committal to His purposes.

David would be acquiring something, this hundred thousand talents of gold, and then there is the suggestion of all it cost for our individual redemption, for the redemption of a people pleasurable to the blessed God, in this great abundance of silver, all these features shining in the manhood and death of Jesus. Having acquired all this substance through experience with God, through the great

sorrows through which he passed, and through the great victories which he won. David was constantly acquiring something, but always having in mind the great issue of his life. Our brother was asking whether the great issue of our lives is to be that we are assembly persons.
The great issue of David’s life was that there might be palatial conditions for the blessed God. “This palace is not to be for man, but for Jehovah Elohim”, he tells the people (1
Chronicles 29: 1), involving conditions suitable for the blessed God. This is for Jehovah Elohim, not for man, and so he looked for Solomon to add to what he had acquired.

It is open to each one of us, beloved brethren, to be adding something as we all receive. If we add anything, it is of what we have received. We often hear of the names that Pharaoh gave to Joseph, but his mother gave him his personal name, meaning, “Jehovah will add”, Genesis 30: 24. The Lord Jesus would add something in substance to all our souls which is to be contributive for His pleasure here, for the pleasure of God, and for the upbuilding of the saints. How glorious the things David acquired! The whole thing became illumined; the glory of God descended upon all that David acquired. We read in the last chapter of this book of the willing-heartedness of the giving, the fulness of all that was secured. Solomon was to add to it, and I believe the Lord would say to each one of us, as assembly persons, that we should be adding something, concerned to add constantly on assembly occasions, on every occasion, not only orally but in our spirits. The brothers speak, the sisters do not speak, but surely they are adding something in the state of their own souls to what is pleasurable and suitable to the Lord Jesus. Suitable conditions for Christ would involve every person being pure in their hearts, judging themselves, and enhancing all that is of
Christ.

The other reference was not particularly to Samson but to the swarm of bees. Perhaps that would be characteristically an assembly thought. There had been a great victory—a young lion roared against him, and Samson rent it as a kid. What a victory! It speaks to our hearts of the victory of the Lord Jesus, the glorious Victor. But here are some, we might say, who are exploiting the victory. The swarm of bees takes up residence in the carcase. If there is a great need to add, it relates to the food supply, the sweetness of all that is for Christ, and what is for the saints too. Our brother quoted—
‘All that delights Thy taste
Doth here abound’.

It is what is suitable to the taste of Christ. This swarm of bees was active. The Lord Jesus says, “Observe with attention the lilies of the field”, Matthew 6: 28. I observed with attention, at the end of the summer, just one bee. It was very active, and full of concentration, going from flower to flower, drawing a little sustenance from each. One thing I observed was that it had been on this service for quite a long time. I would say his life had not much longer to go.
When bees are young there is something fresh—a yellow band around the bee—but this one had become shiny and black. Nature itself would teach us.

I just want to draw this allusion—this bee was single-mindedly drawing substance for the hive. Probably he would not partake much of it. He would get a little for himself at the time, but what he was concerned about was that the life of the hive should go on, even when he was no longer there; that honey was to be stored up. It just seemed an illustration of how each one of us would be devotedly thinking of

what was for the good of the assembly, for the glory of Christ. Even nature would teach us as to the activities which should mark us, just one bee adding a little to the stock which was to provide food and sweetness. O, beloved brethren, could we each be doing that from our hearts, adding something of sweetness and food?
The last suggestion is Paul. Paul liked to be doing something. I just got that impression today.

When he was struck down on the Damascus road, when the Lord Jesus appeared to him, he said, “Who art thou, Lord?”. That was his first question. He got an impression of the greatness of the Man in the glory which altered his life completely, and filled his soul; but the second thing he asked was, “What shall I do, Lord?” (Acts 22: 10); Paul characteristically was always doing something.

Here, you might say, is the aftermath of the shipwreck. Paul had been doing many things; he had embraced the young man who fell, bringing in warmth there; he had been helping the saints in every possible way, but here is the shipwreck. We have known something of public shipwrecks too. I read the end of Acts 27 to suggest the kind of persons who were there—

“The counsel of the soldiers was that they should kill the prisoners, lest any one should swim off and escape”. The men who would have killed Paul, and the centurion who was desirous of saving him, all were brought safe to land, every one. Is there resentment in Paul’s heart against these men? They all got safe to land, some swimming some on boards. Some think that Paul was a swimmer. Sometimes I like to think of Paul as on a board. Of certain persons it is said that they are gallant independents; I always think Paul was a gallant dependent. I think as he was coming ashore he would be saying, ‘“The Son of God, who has loved me

and given himself for me”. We are all going to get safe to land. The blessed One who loved me and gave Himself for me went under the waves. He was in the heart of the seas, at the bottoms of the mountains’. Oh the things the Lord Jesus has done!—I think they would be filling the soul of Paul; not a gallant independent, but a gallant dependent, depending on the Lord Jesus.

And when he gets to land, is he vindictive at all in his spirit? They would have killed Paul, they would have killed all the prisoners, but it says they all got ashore, and Paul’s immediate reaction was to do something to add to the warmth of all. I think in the bundle of sticks he would have some precious thoughts of the manhood of the Lord Jesus to keep this warmth alive among the saints. I will not say more, beloved brethren; may we each One be adding something, characteristically assembly persons, adding something for the pleasure of the Lord Jesus, for the blessing and benefit of the local saints, and for the assembly generally.
May we all be committed to it, for His name’s sake.

Chapters 22 to 26 of Genesis present aspects of Christ’s greatness seen in Isaac. In chapter 22 we have sonship in its perfection—“They went both of them together” (Genesis 22: 6, 8)—wondrously fulfilled in the Lord’s coming here, who could say—“I and the Father are one”, John 10: 30. The reference by Abraham in Genesis 22: 8 to God providing Himself with the sheep indicates Christ’s greatness sacrificially, in line with John the baptist’s testimony to the Lamb of God. In Genesis 24 Isaac typifies Christ where He is, given all things by the Father, so that the servant, a type of the Spirit, owns him to Rebecca as “my master”. The Spirit is sent by Christ as well as by the Father (John 15: 26). In Genesis 25 Abraham permits of no rival in sending away his other seed from Isaac his son, who in chapter 26 receives a hundredfold—“And the man became great, and he became continually greater, until he was very great” (Genesis 26: 13). So Christ must fill everything, as it is said, “Christ everything, and in all”, Colossians 3: 11. He will receive a full yield according to the counsels of the blessed God.
Kingston, Ont.

articles.title: THE KINGDOM OF GOD
articles.author: C. Middleton
articles.place: For those who know and prove that God is love.

paragraphs.text: Can righteousness and peace and joy be found
In this poor world where sin and death abound?
How many as their years of life go by,
Ignore the fact, God’s kingdom has come nigh.
Behold the crowds going heedless on their way,
No thought of God or what He has to say;
And yet amidst them some who have received
Glad tidings of the kingdom and believed.
What wondrous favour when with opened eye
We see the blessings God has brought so nigh.
Into His kingdom we can entrance, make,
A kingdom that no evil power can shake.
Upon the throne is Jesus seated now,
The One to whom soon every knee shall bow.
And here on earth, by owning Jesus’ sway,
We taste the blessings of the coming day.
Here grace abounds and righteousness is known,
Since for their sins the Saviour did atone;
And guilty sinners now are justified
Because their debt was paid when Jesus died.
So in the kingdom they can rightly be
As owning Jesus, that their Lord is He.
The will subdued, what blessing to the soul
Is known when Jesus has complete control.
Here peace is proved, which is not known elsewhere,
The peace that comes from being in His care.
No power of evil have we now to fear,
The power of God, it keeps us safely here.
Here, too, the Spirit does great joy afford
And saints are found rejoicing in the Lord.
This spring of joy thus placed within our hearts
Divinely given joy to us imparts.
It may be tribulation is our part,
Yet nought can touch the joy that’s in the heart.
The blessings of the kingdom nought can move

“PRAISE WAITETH FOR THEE IN SILENCE” The opening words of Psalm 65 no doubt look forward to the glorious millennial revival of the praises of God in Zion; as the hymn says, ‘Yet wider praise in Zion waits for Thee, her Lord and King’. They could also refer to the moments of powerful silence before the service of old began. All would be assembled—the singers, the musicians, the great congregation. All would be ready, and a reverent, holy calm would descend as the moment for the service to commence approached. It would be a silence of power. To use an illustration, if an orchestra were to perform at a given hour, each musician would be in his place, each instrument at concert pitch. Then at the set time all would move into action.

All this bears on the very important matter of how we assemble. We come together for supreme privilege in our assemblings. Each occasion has some relation to the service of God; each relates to the sphere where God Himself dwells and moves. Therefore it becomes us to assemble with preparation, punctuality, reverence, and dignity, so that, under divine impulse, we may move as one into the service.

The Lord’s care of our bodies is involved in that statement in Ephesians 5 (“He is Saviour of the body”); He has constant care of our bodies, and I always refer to the Lord in regard of the body, because it is a kind of peculiar treasure—the bodies of the saints are the peculiar property of the Lord. I think this is the fullest expression of the thought that He is the Saviour of the body.
(J. Taylor, N.S. Vol. 40, p.283)
